opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest open question is really about reliability itself: how do we get from systems that are impressive some of the time to systems you can actually trust to get it right nearly all of the time?

With AlphaGo, we had a very clean setting. The rules were perfectly defined, the reward was unambiguous — you win or you lose — and we had a perfect simulator, so the system could play millions of games against itself and get feedback on every single one. That's what let us push it to superhuman and, crucially, very consistent performance. Search on top of a learned model gave us a way to spend more compute at decision time and reliably get better answers.

LLM-based agents live in a much messier world. The environments are open-ended, the reward is often fuzzy or delayed, and you don't have a perfect simulator of the internet or of a user's codebase or of a business workflow. So the question becomes: what's the equivalent of self-play and search in that setting? How do you build verifiers or reward signals that are good enough that the model can actually learn from its own experience without just exploiting holes in the reward?

And related to that is compounding errors. An agent taking fifty or a hundred steps needs each step to be extremely reliable, otherwise small mistakes snowball. In Go, search helped catch and correct those mistakes. For agents, we're still figuring out how to give them that ability to plan, check their own work, and recover gracefully.

So if I had to name one thing, it's this: can we bring the kind of reliability we got from reinforcement learning and search in closed domains into these open-ended, real-world domains? I'm optimistic, but I think that's where most of the hard, interesting work is right now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts LLM-based systems that succeed only some of the time with AlphaGo’s consistent performance, framing the gap as reaching reliable success nearly all the time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest open question is reliability itself, and specifically what it would take to get an LLM-based agent to the point where you can actually trust it the way you could trust AlphaGo.

With AlphaGo, we had a very clear picture of why the system was reliable. It had a well-defined environment, a well-defined reward, and it could search. If the policy network suggested a move that looked good but was actually bad, the search would usually catch it, because it would play the position forward and see that the evaluation collapsed. And then the whole loop reinforced itself: the search made the policy better, the better policy made the search more efficient. By the time it played Lee Sedol, we had millions of self-play games and a very good sense of its win rate. Reliability wasn't a hope, it was something we had measured.

Agents built on language models are in a completely different situation. The environment is open-ended, the reward is often ambiguous or only available much later, and most of the time there is no real search in the loop. The model produces a plan, maybe it produces some reasoning, and then it acts. If it makes a mistake early in a long task, there is often nothing that catches it, and the error compounds. That is the opposite of what we had in Go, where every step was checked against the actual dynamics of the game.

So the open question, to me, is: how do you get the equivalent of search and verification into these systems? Part of that is learning good world models, so the agent can simulate consequences before committing. Part of it is learning value functions for messy, real-world tasks, so the agent has some sense of "this is going badly" before it finishes. And part of it is grounding, making sure the thing the model is optimising against actually corresponds to what we want, because in Go the game tells you the truth and in the real world nothing does that for you automatically.

If we solve that, I think you get agents that improve themselves in the way AlphaGo did, through experience rather than just through more human data. If we don't, you get systems that are impressive in demos but that you can never quite depend on, and I think that gap between impressive and dependable is really the whole problem right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad reliability gap and contrasts AlphaGo’s measured win rate with error-prone LLM agents, but it does not identify inconsistent success across repeated attempts as the gap.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest open question is how we get these agents to be reliable over long sequences of decisions. An LLM can produce a very impressive answer, but if you ask it to carry out a task that requires many steps, even small errors can accumulate.

With AlphaGo, we had a very clear environment, a clear objective, and the ability to play games and learn from the outcome. For an agent operating in the real world, those things are much less well defined. How do you know whether it has actually succeeded? How does it recognise that it has made a mistake, and recover?

So the question for me is whether we can build a learning process that turns a system that can often do something into a system that can consistently do it. That gap between capability and reliability is really important.

r001.rationale: The response frames the gap as moving from a system that can often do something to one that can consistently do it, and discusses that gap in comparison with AlphaGo.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest open question is how we get from an agent that can do something impressive once to an agent that can do it reliably. With AlphaGo, you had a very clear objective, a precise set of rules, and the ability to play games and measure whether you were improving. You could also use search to spend more computation checking a decision before committing to it.

With LLM-based agents, the environment is much less constrained. The goals can be ambiguous, and a mistake early in a long sequence of actions can affect everything that follows. So the question is whether we can build a learning and evaluation loop that gives us that same confidence: can the agent recognize when it is wrong, recover, and consistently finish the task? I think reinforcement learning and search are promising ingredients, but making that work across open-ended tasks is still a major challenge.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts an agent that succeeds impressively once with one that can perform reliably, and asks whether LLM agents can consistently finish tasks—clearly expressing inconsistent success across attempts as the reliability gap.
